Small Town, Big Float
Two rivals. One flatbed. The biggest float in town, and it can't turn a corner.
A designer home from the city and the town mechanic enter rival parade floats, end up sharing one, and build the least turnable moon in history.

Luis came home to Carver's Bend after his city job folded, and he'd like one thing here to be bigger than people remember. Beau runs the only garage with a covered bay, so both their parade floats end up in it, and then on his trailer, and then stuck at the corner of Main and Elm. You decide what Luis cuts, whose name goes on the plate, and whether the seat next to Beau is a designer's seat or a date.
A festival volunteer on the paint crew — one of the six people who actually painted the thing.
If nobody bends, the float never makes the route, and Luis leaves town proving the one thing he was afraid of.

The Moon Is Stuck
Get the moon out of the door — somehow
Tillman Auto, bay two
Monday, 5:30 PM — five days to the parade
Five days before the Harvest Lights Parade, two rival floats share one garage, because Tillman Auto has the only covered bay in Carver's Bend.
Luis's moon, eight feet of plywood, foam and LED strip, is wedged in the bay door at a forty-degree angle.
Your moon violates several laws of physics.
It was supposed to look ambitious.
It looks stuck.
I push. The moon groans. A small piece of crescent falls onto my shoe, which feels symbolic.
I set down my coffee and look at the door rail, then the moon, then him. One of the three has to give.
What gives?
Cut the moon down. Admit it's too big.
Fine. Take a foot off the bottom. Two. Don't tell me which.
I trim it clean. When it clears the door, I pat the flatbed. Put it on my trailer. Yours doesn't have brakes.
By nightfall there's one float in bay two instead of two. Nobody tells the committee.
Luis let Beau cut the moon down to fit; the two rival floats merged onto Beau's trailer.
Pull the door rail instead — on his terms.
Rail comes off. It costs me tomorrow morning, and you're holding the ladder.
Deal. I'm an excellent ladder holder. Ask anyone.
The moon clears the door whole. Beau's schedule doesn't. Luis owes him a morning, and they both know it.
And it rides on my trailer. Yours doesn't have brakes.
Beau took the door rail down so the moon could stay whole; Luis owes him a morning, and the floats merged on Beau's trailer.
Keep it whole. Drag it out yourself.
It stays whole. I'll take it out through the side lot.
The side lot is gravel and a fence.
It takes me, my cousin and three hours. The moon survives. My dignity stays somewhere on the gravel.
At ten that night, Beau leaves the bay light on and a note taped to the moon: TRAILER'S YOURS IF YOU WANT BRAKES.
Luis kept the moon whole and hauled it out himself; Beau left the light on and offered his trailer anyway.
Bigger Than They Remembered
Say what coming home actually scares him about
The workbench, bay two
Tuesday, 9:40 PM
One float now: Beau's flatbed, Luis's moon, a paint crew that went home at nine. The space heater clanks. Luis is re-gluing glitter he already glued.
You've been doing that same inch since eight.
Everyone at the diner asks what happened in the city. Like I'm a weather report. Like something did.
I wanted one thing here to be bigger than they remembered.
You could've started with lunch.

How much does Luis tell him?
Tell him the whole truth about the city.

I nod once. I don't make it a big thing. I push the other half of the sandwich across.
Thursday, after close, we take her out on the real route. Empty street. Just us and the moon.
Luis told Beau his studio folded and he's home for good; Beau invited him to a late-night trial run on the real route.
Eat first. Tell him a little.
Short version: the city was expensive and I got tired. Long version needs more sandwich.
Long version after the trial run, then. Thursday night. Real route, empty street, pie after.
Luis eats the entire thing. He doesn't remember deciding to.
Luis gave Beau the short version and saved the rest for after Thursday's trial run.
Change the subject back to the float.
Anyway. Can the trailer take the weight if I add a second star?
I let the subject change. I'm good at waiting at red lights.
No second star. But Thursday, after close, we test her on Main Street and find out what she can take.
Luis steered back to the float; Beau let it go and set a Thursday night trial run.
Pick a Side
Change the design or the route — together
Corner of Main and Elm
Thursday, 11:15 PM
Main Street after eleven: one blinking light, a closed bank, and a float that has just discovered the corner of Main and Elm is ninety degrees.
I stop the truck with the moon's left horn six inches from the bank's awning. Nobody breathes.
I'm on the ground with a flashlight, waving him left. He's already steering right.
Pick a side. We can't pull in opposite directions.
That felt personal.
It was about the steering. Mostly.
Either the moon gets smaller or the route changes. Changing the route means knocking on doors on Birch Street.
How do they get around the corner?
Shrink the moon. Give the corner room.
Take another foot off. Tilt the horns in. It'll still read as a moon.
It'll read as a moon that fits.
By 1 AM the float clears the corner with a hand's width to spare. Luis sketches the smaller moon on a napkin and, grudgingly, likes it.
Luis agreed to shrink the moon again; the float cleared the corner of Main and Elm.
Reroute down Birch — ask the neighbors first.
Keep the moon. Go down Birch instead. We ask the three houses on Birch first. Tomorrow, with pie.
Pie is a strong opening.
By Friday noon, all three households say yes, and one asks to ride. The route gets longer. The committee gets a signed note.
They kept the moon and rerouted down Birch Street after all three households agreed.
Keep the design. Force the corner.
The design stays. Take it slower.
I try it at walking speed. The horn catches the awning and tears off a strip of canvas.
That's a bill, Luis. Yours or mine, it's still a bill.
They leave a note on the bank's door. The moon stays full size, and Beau goes quiet in a way that isn't a joke.
Luis refused to change the design; the moon tore the bank's awning and Beau went quiet.
Whose Float
Credit everyone who built it — for real
Bay two, the float's tailgate
Friday, 6:00 PM
The committee wants a nameplate by seven. I paint BEAU TILLMAN on the board first, before I can think about it.
I take the brush and add six names underneath: the paint crew, in the order they showed up.
Your shop made it possible.
And six people painted it.
There goes my dramatic signature.
You can still sign.
Smaller?
Readable. Like the moon.
How does Luis sign?
Sign small, at the bottom, readable.
I sign at the bottom, in my plainest hand. Four seconds. The hardest lettering I've done all year.
Looks good. Looks like a team.
Luis signed the nameplate small, under Beau and the six volunteers.
Ask the crew how they want credit.
Before anything's final: does the crew want their names on it? Real names, in public?
Two say yes. Three want first names only. One asks to be listed as The Guy With The Ladder. Luis letters all of it, exactly.
Best nameplate in the parade.
Luis asked each volunteer how they wanted to be credited and lettered the nameplate exactly that way.
Keep your big signature.
I paint NAVARRO across the top in letters a foot tall. It looks incredible. It looks like I built this alone.
Then the crew goes on the front. They painted the front.
Beau doesn't argue further. He carries the ladder to the other end himself and doesn't hand Luis the brush again.
Luis put his own name across the top in huge letters; Beau moved the crew's names to the front and stopped handing him the brush.
They Don't Care About the Moon
Make room for the riders and finish the route
The staging lot behind the Grange hall
Saturday, 6:20 PM — forty minutes to lineup
The riders arrive: eight regulars from the senior center, promised a seat on a float, carrying their own cushions.
Mrs. Pruitt, eighty-one, pats the deck and asks where the chairs go. There is no room for chairs. The moon is where the chairs go.
I watch them look straight past the moon, at the string lights down Main, the way you look at something you've waited all year for.
They don't care about the moon.
I do. We worked hard on that ridiculous thing.
I'm already unbolting the back half of the deck, measuring folding chairs with my eyes.
What goes on the deck?
Small moon up front. Chairs for everyone.
We slide the moon to the front corner. It lights their faces from behind, which, honestly, is better design.
Eight chairs, strapped and checked twice by Beau. The float takes the route at walking pace, and the riders wave like royalty.
They moved the small moon to the front and gave all eight riders a strapped-in seat for the whole route.
Ask the riders what they want.
Mrs. Pruitt. Moon in the middle, or the better view?
The riders vote with great seriousness. Chairs win, seven to one. The one wants the moon close enough to touch.
I bolt the moon at arm's reach from her seat. Safety strap first. She touches it the whole way down Main.
The riders voted for chairs; Beau bolted the moon within reach of the one rider who wanted to touch it.
Keep the moon center stage.
The moon is the float. We'll fit four chairs around it.
Four safe chairs. Not eight. I don't strap people in where I can't reach them.
Four riders go. Four watch from the curb with their cushions. Mrs. Pruitt waves anyway. Luis feels it all the way down Main.
Luis kept the moon at center; only four riders fit safely, and four watched from the curb.

Bay two, after the parade
Saturday, 9:30 PM

I hold my hands up under the shop light. Silver to the wrist. The glitter is in my knuckles, my watchband, possibly my soul.

The Moon Lights Up Twice
Answer the invitation clearly — even with a bus to catch
The empty lot behind the feed store
The next Saturday, 7:45 PM
A week later, the float sits in the lot behind the feed store. Folding chairs face a bedsheet screen strung between two poles.
Someone brought a projector. Someone brought popcorn. The moon glows at the edge of it all, doing absolutely nothing, perfectly.
It finally turns without moving.
A triumph of design.
Want the seat next to me?
As the designer?
As my date. If you say yes.
What does Luis say?
Say yes. As his date.
That's the best specification yet. Yes.
I don't put my arm around his chair. I rest it on the armrest between us and leave it there. Available.
Twenty minutes into the movie, Luis's hand finds it.

Take the seat — as the designer.

The lot behind the feed store
